title: Can you prove AI ROI in Software Eng? (Stanford 120k Devs Study) – Yegor Denisov-Blanch, Stanford

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is measuring AI ROI in software engineering through novel evaluation methodology, ML-based engineering output metrics, and benchmark frameworks rather than building a specific system. The research studies coding assistants across 600+ companies and developer platforms, with the AI Engineering Practices Benchmark and maturity levels directly targeting developer tooling contexts. The entire presentation concerns evaluation methodology—how to measure AI impact, design metrics, and benchmark engineering practices. Requires familiarity with software engineering metrics, ML evaluation concepts, and statistical correlation analysis, but remains accessible to a practitioner audience. A Stanford researcher presenting empirical findings and a measurement framework at the AI Engineer conference. All claims are directly stated in the transcript with quantitative backing from the two-year study.

summary: Yegor Denisov-Blanch presents Stanford research on AI ROI in software engineering, covering 120k+ developers across 600+ companies over two years. The methodology uses ML models trained on millions of expert panel evaluations to assess code commits on implementation time, maintainability, and complexity, enabling scalable measurement. A matched comparison of 46 AI-using teams vs. 46 non-AI teams shows a median 10% productivity gain as of July, with a widening gap between top and bottom performers suggesting a rich-get-richer compounding effect. Investigation of driving factors reveals that AI usage (token spend) has only a loose 0.20 linear correlation with productivity, with a death valley effect around 10 million tokens. Environment cleanliness—combining tests, types, documentation, modularity, and code quality—shows a stronger R²=0.40 correlation with AI productivity gains. The research introduces an AI Engineering Practices Benchmark that scans codebases for AI fingerprints, categorizing usage from level 0 (no AI) to level 4 (agentic orchestration). A case study of one company shows two business units with identical AI access had vastly different adoption rates (40% vs. lower), demonstrating access alone doesn't guarantee effective use. For ROI measurement, business outcomes are too noisy with confounding variables, so engineering outcomes are proposed instead. The framework uses a primary metric (engineering output via ML expert panel model, not lines of code or PR counts) plus guardrail metrics across rework/refactoring, quality/tech/risk, and people/devops categories. Guardrails should be maintained at healthy levels, not maximized. A detailed case study of a 350-person team illustrates the framework: after AI adoption, PRs increased 14% but code quality decreased 9% and became more erratic, rework increased 2.5x, and effective output remained flat—suggesting potentially negative ROI that PR-count metrics alone would have missed entirely. The company should use this data to improve rather than abandon AI. The talk concludes with an invitation for companies, especially those with Cursor Enterprise access, to participate in ongoing research at Stanford.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Methodology: ML Panels of Experts
sections.summary: Companies spend millions on AI tools but enterprise effectiveness is unclear. Two-year research uses time series (git history) and cross-sectional data across companies. ML model replicates panels of 10-15 human experts evaluating code commits on implementation time, maintainability, and complexity, trained on millions of evaluations.

sections.title: Four Key Topics Overview
sections.summary: Presentation covers four areas: factors driving AI productivity gains, AI practices benchmark, measuring AI ROI, and a case study.

sections.title: Case Study: 10% Productivity Gain & The Widening Gap
sections.summary: 46 AI-using teams matched with 46 non-AI teams show median 10% productivity gain as of July. Widening gap between top and bottom performers suggests rich-get-richer compounding. Leaders must know their cohort position to course-correct.

sections.title: Factors Driving Performance: Usage vs. Quality
sections.summary: Token usage shows loose 0.20 linear correlation with productivity, with a death valley around 10 million tokens. Conclusion: AI usage quality matters more than usage volume.

sections.title: The Environment Cleanliness Index
sections.summary: Composite index of tests, types, documentation, modularity, and code quality shows R²=0.40 correlation with AI productivity gains. Invest in codebase hygiene to unlock AI benefits.

sections.title: Managing Codebase Entropy & AI Trust
sections.summary: Clean code amplifies AI gains. Unchecked AI use accelerates codebase entropy, degrading cleanliness. Engineers must know when to use AI; rejected outputs collapse trust and further reduce gains.

sections.title: AI Engineering Practices Benchmark & Fingerprinting
sections.summary: Benchmark scans codebases for AI fingerprints, quantifying usage patterns monthly via git history. Maturity levels from 0 (no AI) to 4 (agentic orchestration). Open-source tool available via sweeper research portal.

sections.title: Case Study: Unequal Adoption Across Business Units
sections.summary: One company's two business units with identical AI access showed different adoption rates—one at 40% usage, the other lagging. Access doesn't guarantee effective use; leaders must understand how engineers use AI.

sections.title: Challenges in Measuring AI ROI via Business Outcomes
sections.summary: Business outcomes have too much noise and confounding variables. Engineering outcomes provide clearer signal but assume product can direct capacity into value, engineering is a bottleneck, and proxy metrics are still useful despite imperfection. Goodhart's law guarded by balanced metrics and healthy culture.

sections.title: Proposed Measurement Framework: Usage & Outcomes
sections.summary: Two parts: measure usage (access-based vs. usage-based, with usage-based telemetry as gold standard) and measure engineering outcomes. Can retroactively measure impact using git history. Vendor APIs differ in granularity.

sections.title: Metric Framework: Primary Output vs. Guardrails
sections.summary: Primary metric is engineering output via ML expert panel model, not lines of code, PR counts, or DORA. Guardrail metrics across rework/refactoring, quality/tech/risk, and people/devops should be maintained healthy, not maximized.

sections.title: Case Study: AI Adoption's Negative Impact on Quality
sections.summary: A 350-person team adopted AI in May. Four months before and after showed PRs up 14% but code quality down 9% and more erratic. Rework increased 2.5x while effective output stayed flat. Had the company only measured PR counts, they would have falsely concluded success. The ROI may be negative, but the company should use the data to improve rather than abandon AI. The talk concludes with an invitation for companies, especially Cursor Enterprise users, to participate in research at softwareengineeringproductivity.stanford.edu.
